title: Miniature Garden Resin Charms: Plan a Woodland Scene
description: Build a miniature garden layout with mushroom, tree-stump, leaf and flower resin charms. Plan scale, color, attachment and a repeatable project list.
answer: Start a miniature garden with one focal piece, a small group of supporting shapes and an open path through the scene. Dry-fit the actual components on your chosen base before fixing anything. Compare dimensions, back shapes and attachment points for each SKU; a shared woodland theme does not mean the pieces share a miniature scale.
heroCaption: RW21765 pastel mushroom cabochons: a starting point for a soft woodland palette. See the product page for the shown assortment.
sections: Choose the story before the components

A miniature garden becomes easier to arrange when you can describe it in a sentence: a quiet mushroom clearing, a flower stall beside a stump, or a tiny vegetable patch. Pick the setting first, then give each component a role. The focal piece is where the eye should land. Supporting pieces explain the setting. Small accents connect those pieces without filling every gap. This approach helps you decide what to leave out when several attractive designs compete for the same space.

For a first layout, use a removable tray, shallow display box or another base you can test on the table. Trace its usable outline on paper and mark any rim, lid or handle that the finished decoration must clear. Keep the scene inside that boundary. A design that looks balanced on an open tabletop may feel crowded once it is inside its actual frame.
Shortlist real products by their role

Try RW21765 pastel mushrooms as the focal group and RW26810 tree-stump miniatures as a contrasting woodland form. RW26817 miniature flower bouquets can suggest a garden corner or small flower stall. RW26811 green leaves offer another plant motif, but this listing includes holes: inspect the hole position and decide whether that detail belongs in your scene. These are design starting points from the catalog, rather than a packaged kit or a promise that every component will fit together.

If you prefer a vegetable-patch story, compare the pig and cabbage designs in RW20809 instead. Keep their shapes visible rather than burying them under other accents. Note the exact SKU beside each paper cutout or trial component so you can reproduce the arrangement later. Similar product names are easy to confuse when a project has several shades or mixed designs.
Check scale from measurements, then test the silhouette

Compare the stated dimensions on the individual product pages and request clarification for any dimension you need to make the layout work. Front photographs alone cannot establish height, depth, weight or the shape of the back. A mushroom can look small in a close-up and still dominate your chosen base. A tree stump may occupy more floor space than its front view suggests. Ask for a side or rear view when the attachment surface matters.

Cut paper shapes to the confirmed footprints, arrange them on the base and photograph the result from the intended viewing angle. Use the actual samples before final assembly, because paper cannot show how a rounded back sits or whether a tall piece hides another motif. Keep a visible route between the groups. Negative space gives the scene a readable structure and makes individual details easier to enjoy.
Build a palette around one existing component

Take a color that is already present in your focal piece and repeat it in one supporting area. A soft pink mushroom might pair with a quieter green accent and an off-white base. You can also choose a stronger contrast, provided the brightest detail remains where you want attention. There is no required color ratio; the useful test is whether the arrangement still reads clearly when viewed at its final size.

Adobe's color-wheel tool offers analogous, complementary and other harmony options. Use it to explore a palette, then return to the physical samples. A screen palette is a planning aid, not a specification for the resin colors you will receive. Photograph your dry fit under consistent light, and avoid choosing a new background simply because it matches an edited product photograph.
Match the fixing method to the actual surfaces

Keep the first arrangement loose until you have checked how each component sits. A flatback, a dimensional ornament and a drilled leaf may need different attachment choices. Do not assume that every decorative piece can be threaded, glued upright or attached to a flexible base. Check the product description and ask about the back or hole when needed. If you use a removable display arrangement, test that pieces stay in place during normal handling.

For a bonded project, select an adhesive whose manufacturer lists both surfaces as suitable. Aleene's FAQ explains that the surfaces being joined affect glue choice and that dirt or grease can interfere with adhesion. Follow the instructions for your selected formula, including preparation, application, ventilation and curing. Make a small trial with the same base and a sample component before committing the whole scene. This guide does not establish adhesive compatibility for any SKU.
Turn the successful dry fit into a repeatable project

Once you like the layout, record the base size, component codes, chosen variants and the number of pieces actually used. Take one overhead photograph and one image from the normal viewing direction. Mark where the focal piece sits relative to the base edge so a second version is easier to assemble. If you are preparing a workshop or a small collection, write down which details can vary and which ones define the design.

Keep the shopping list separate from the project recipe. A supplier's bag quantity is an ordering unit, while the number of pieces used in one scene is your own design choice. Ask about the available assortment before promising that every project will contain an identical mushroom or flower. Decorative components are non-edible craft materials. Choose an appropriate audience and storage arrangement, and keep food-like designs separate from food. For product selection or a mixed order, send the finished trial photo together with the exact SKU list.

title: Candy Decoden Layout: Choose Charms Before You Glue
description: Plan a candy-themed decoden layout with sugar-style cabochons and bear or cherry accents. Check color, spacing, back shape and adhesive compatibility.
answer: Plan candy decoden around a clear focal motif, a controlled palette and the usable area of the actual base. Arrange the charms without adhesive first, leaving functional openings and comfortable edges clear. Confirm the back shape and test your chosen adhesive on both materials before making the finished decoration.
heroCaption: RW340 sugar-style resin cabochons. These are decorative craft components, not edible candy.
sections: Give the layout a clear focal point

A candy-themed decoration can become visually busy before you have used many pieces. Start by choosing the motif you want someone to notice first: a bear, a cherry grouping or a cluster of sugar-style shapes. Place that focal group on the empty base and check it from a normal viewing distance. Then add supporting pieces in stages. You do not need to use every design in a mixed assortment to make the theme recognizable.

Choose the base before buying the whole range. A display plaque, a box lid and a phone-case blank have different handling requirements and different usable areas. Sketch the outline at actual size, including edges, hinges, openings and raised features. If the base is used with another object, check the combined fit during the trial rather than relying on a flat outline alone.
Compare three different candy-style roles

RW340 sugar candy resin flatback cabochons provide a textured candy-style motif. RW1021 transparent sugar-cube cabochons offer a different visual effect, while RW002852 bear and cherry flatback charms can introduce recognizable character and fruit accents. Compare the individual listings and samples before deciding which one should lead. These are separate catalog products; their shared theme does not establish identical dimensions, a matching finish or a ready-made set.

For an initial composition, choose one main product and one supporting product. Add a third only if it solves a visible gap in the design. A cube-like shape can create a quiet area beside a more detailed focal charm, while a bear or cherry can make the theme easier to read. Keep the chosen SKU, image and variant together in your project notes so a later order refers to the same component.
Use the actual base as a spacing template

Dry-fit with physical samples whenever possible. Keep the perimeter comfortable to hold and check that no component overhangs an edge where it could catch during use. For a phone-case project, leave camera, flash, buttons, speaker openings and connector access clear. Check compatibility with your own device and accessories. A decorative layout is not a claim of device protection, impact performance or compatibility with charging equipment.

Move the arrangement through the positions it will encounter in normal use. Look at a box lid when it is open as well as closed. Check a plaque from its display angle. For a handled item, see where fingers rest and whether a raised charm sits in that space. If the trial feels crowded, remove a supporting piece before reaching for smaller fillers. Open space can be a deliberate part of the design.
Choose color from samples rather than names

Terms such as pastel, candy pink and clear describe a direction, not an exact color match. Begin with the focal component you have in hand and choose a background that lets its edges remain visible. Repeat a supporting color in a second area to connect the composition. Transparent and translucent pieces can look different over a dark base, a light base or an adhesive layer, so inspect the actual combination before fixing it.

Adobe's color-wheel tool can help compare analogous and complementary palette directions. Use those options to explore alternatives without treating a screen color as a supplier's shade specification. Save the palette beside a photograph of your physical trial. If consistency across several finished pieces matters, request confirmation of the available colors and assortment rather than assuming that a mixed bag will give you the same combination each time.
Treat bonding as its own sample test

Confirm the back shape, base material and intended adhesive before making the final piece. A product described as a flatback still needs to sit correctly on your particular base. A rigid cabochon on a flexible blank creates a different assembly from the same piece on a rigid display board. Do not infer a bonding method from a styled photograph or assume that a decorative cream medium will behave like every other adhesive.

Aleene's FAQ ties glue choice to the surfaces being joined and identifies surface contamination as one reason a bond can fail. Read the instructions for the exact formula you select and follow its preparation, application and curing guidance. Test an unobtrusive area or spare base with a sample charm. Check for staining, clouding, movement and unwanted marks after the stated cure period. There is no universal curing time or glue recommendation for all resin finishes and case materials.
Save the recipe before making a batch

Photograph the completed dry fit, then make a simple placement record: base reference, component SKU, selected design, quantity used and any spacing you want to repeat. Keep adhesive details and the results of your trial with that record. Assemble one complete sample before preparing multiple decorated blanks. This gives you a chance to discover an awkward edge or a change in appearance before repeating it across the whole project.

For kits, distinguish the components included from tools, adhesive and instructions that must be supplied separately. State when the arrangement can vary, and do not illustrate a fixed assortment unless you can provide it. Keep the food-like theme clearly decorative: these components are not edible and should be stored away from food. If you are choosing products for resale or an activity, confirm audience suitability and destination requirements separately. Send Qula Craft your trial image, SKU list, required quantities and preferred packing when you are ready to discuss an order.
